A1.justification: Despite retitling and extensive reorganization, both PDFs describe the same QA fine-tuning and Physics Context Builders work. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices A–C support a complete comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Falling Tower and CLEVRER experiments, Sim2Real evaluation, PCB routing results, and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experimental results and adds Falling Tower studies of training-question composition and training-data quantity.

M1.justification: Both versions use PaliGemma-3B with LoRA for QA answering and PCB description generation, retain human narration and structured physics formats, and integrate PCBs through contextual prompting and triage. The stronger emphasis on perception–reasoning separation does not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both use CLEVRER and Falling Tower, including the same 20-image real-world evaluation. Falling Tower's predictive questions are renamed stability questions. The exact 4,864-scene and 72,775-question counts emphasized in v2 already appear in v1 Appendix C.

E2.justification: v2 removes untuned PaliGemma-3B from the main benchmark comparisons, although its Falling Tower simulation scores remain in the new ablation table. Section 3.2 adds a numerical comparison with quoted ALOE results. The other principal comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds Falling Tower protocols varying QA subsets and training-data fractions from 1% to 100%. Existing splits and training hyperparameters remain unchanged. Its binary-question description also drops v1's predictive-question exception; unchanged main and appendix scores leave the actual predictive-question handling unclear.

E4.justification: New Table 3 and Figure 3 substantially expand the investigation of training-data dependence, testing transfer between descriptive and stability questions and their different data requirements. Earlier question-framing, training-duration, and vision-freezing ablations are retained; the last moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix B.3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars for these experiments. The new curves follow the existing point-estimate reporting practice; average performance summaries do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark and earlier ablation values remain unchanged. New results concern QA subsets and data fractions; stability-only training achieves 84.4% object and 86.5% tower accuracy. Some untuned-baseline and triage precision/abstention results disappear. v2 also corrects the narration comparison to favor human narration, consistent with both versions' tables.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The training-loss description and evaluation-metric definitions are substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: v1 presents two novel approaches and lists QA fine-tuning as a central contribution. v2 makes the PCB framework and analysis of perception versus reasoning the principal contributions, treating QA fine-tuning as a motivating study with task-specific limitations. Simulation-based learning and Sim2Real claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about QA-specific transfer, task-dependent data efficiency, and the limits of increasing data without diversity. Sections 5–6 develop the distinction between improved perception and remaining reasoning failures, explicitly constrain generalization beyond rigid-body/stability benchmarks, and discuss composing PCBs for multiple phenomena.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies three shapes and five colors and explicitly describes evaluating the final answer after reasoning. It omits v1's shared-LoRA routing implementation detail and exact Gemini-1.5-Pro-002 identifier. Appendix hyperparameters, hardware, compute times, description templates, and dataset-link targets remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially revised around physical reasoning and modular augmentation. v2 adds a substantive comparison with concurrent PhysBench, distinguishing specialized simulation-trained PCBs from generic perception tools, and introduces sources including ALOE, ContPhy, multimodal chain-of-thought, and human physical cognition while removing several earlier references.

P1.justification: The title changes from Synthetic Vision to Physics Context Builders. The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. QA studies precede a dedicated PCB section, discussion and limitations become separate sections, and the vision-module ablation moves into the appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column main layout, redraws the pipeline and triage diagrams, and splits the two combined benchmark tables into separate QA and PCB tables. It adds an ablation table, learning curves, and a description-format display, and combines the appendix distributions into a redesigned two-panel figure.

improvement.justification: Table 3 and Figure 3 provide useful evidence about QA composition and data requirements that v1 lacked. Clearer presentation and more explicit applicability limits improve the paper's assessability. These gains outweigh limited losses in transparency from removing untuned-baseline and triage-abstention details, although the less explicit predictive-question protocol remains a drawback.
